model.name: Governed BR review assistant - idea to production
model.question: Can a business requirement be trusted to pass the kick-off gate, and is the assistant that says so itself trustworthy?
model.summary: An anonymised worked example of a governed LLM assistant that reviews business requirements, modelled end to end: what it is allowed to do, the prompt and template assets that carry the behaviour, how those assets reach a retrieval index at runtime, and the nine-stage delivery pipeline it sits inside. It is built from a real system prompt and a real delivery-process map, with the operator, the assistant codename, the integration partner, the internal committee, the environment names, the channel names and the mode-trigger keyword all removed. The reason it is worth opening is that the source prompt contradicts itself three times and nobody had put the pairs side by side: the full-analysis mode is told both to emit a markdown report ending in a JSON payload and to emit nothing but relayed HTML; a global guardrail forbids producing HTML at all; and the topic guardrail fixes a single-language refusal that the language rule says should mirror the input. It deliberately leaves the score claim unevidenced. Every number on the dashboard the funding board reads derives from three severity coefficients with no stated derivation and no calibration set, and that is the finding this model exists to teach. It does not model the dashboard's own internals, the retrieval ranking, or any customer data.

layers.name: Governance and intent
layers.role: What the assistant is for, what it must refuse, and the rules that decide a verdict. NOT how it is wired together, and NOT the delivery pipeline it sits inside.

layers.name: Prompt and knowledge assets
layers.role: The artefacts that carry the behaviour: the system prompt, the output contracts, the validators and the chapter template they check. NOT the platform they are uploaded to.

layers.name: Runtime wiring
layers.role: The platform objects and the calls between them when a request arrives, including how documents reach the knowledge index. NOT what those documents contain, and NOT who approved them.

layers.name: Idea to production
layers.role: The delivery pipeline the assistant sits inside, stage by stage, with its gates and the role accountable for each. NOT the internals of the assistant.

nodes.label: Linguistic forensics on business requirements
nodes.note: Extract explicit rules from document text, surface logical conflicts, identify operational gaps that block development. The capability is deliberately narrow: it reads, it does not design.

nodes.label: Only what is written exists
nodes.note: Strictly text-bound. No assumptions, no extrapolation. This is what separates a finding from an impression, and it is the reason a missing rule is reportable rather than guessable.

nodes.label: Not a technical architect
nodes.note: The assistant does not propose designs. Stated in the identity section and enforced by the scope control.

nodes.label: Topic restriction
nodes.note: Anything not about business requirements gets one fixed refusal and no engagement with the content. The refusal text is specified in one language only.

nodes.label: HTML restriction

props.quote: Never write HTML tags or generate HTML output autonomously in any response.

nodes.note: Never write HTML tags or generate HTML output autonomously. The dashboard HTML is produced exclusively by the downstream flow.

nodes.label: Scope restriction
nodes.note: Do not discuss system architecture, API design, technical schemas or deployment plans under any circumstances.

nodes.label: A verdict may be BLOCKED for three reasons only
nodes.note: Contradiction between two written rules; conflict between two uploaded documents; a core business rule entirely absent. Both sides of a contradiction must be quoted exactly.

nodes.label: Template gaps are findings, not blockers
nodes.note: Empty template sections, missing names, placeholder use cases and missing secondary metrics are findings. This rule is what stops the verdict inflating.

nodes.label: Score arithmetic: 100 minus 15 / 8 / 3 per finding
nodes.note: Start at 100 and subtract per finding by severity. The three coefficients are stated without a derivation anywhere in the source prompt.

nodes.label: Four readiness dimensions
nodes.note: business = scope and model clarity; it = use cases, lifecycle, integrations; legal = legal, data protection, fraud; operations = reporting, migration, channels. The mapping is asserted; no formula is given for turning chapter findings into a 0-100 figure per dimension.

nodes.label: Mirror the input language; keep labels English
nodes.note: Slovenian in, Slovenian out. English in, English out. Headers, flags and payload key names stay English.

nodes.label: BLOCKED / PARTIALLY CLEAR / CLEARED
nodes.note: The three verdicts. Defined once here so the report, the dashboard payload and the gate all mean the same thing by them.

nodes.label: KICK-OFF READY
nodes.note: Default maturity level, overridden only if the requestor states otherwise.

nodes.label: Validating the BR before kick-off reduces later rework
nodes.note: The reason the assistant exists. Falsifiable: rework after kick-off is countable.

nodes.label: A strictly text-bound reading cannot produce a false blocker
nodes.note: If true, a BLOCKED verdict never needs arguing with. Falsifiable against reviewed cases.

nodes.label: The score coefficients reflect real delivery risk
nodes.note: LOAD-BEARING AND UNEVIDENCED. Every number on the dashboard -- the overall score, the readiness dials, the risk distribution -- is arithmetic over these three coefficients. Nothing in the source states where 15, 8 and 3 came from, and no calibration is referenced. This is the gap the template exists to show: the output is precise, presented as a percentage, and rests on nothing.

nodes.label: A human reviews every BLOCKED verdict before the requestor sees it
nodes.note: Created by the blocker rule. Owned by the business analyst on the delivery side.

nodes.label: Reviewed BR corpus with post-kick-off rework counts
nodes.note: A set of business requirements already through delivery, with the rework each one caused after kick-off and whether the assistant would have flagged it. Settles the rework claim and would also expose a false blocker.

nodes.label: Assistant system prompt
nodes.note: Identity, guardrails, intent detection, initialisation and the two output modes. One document; everything the assistant does is in it.

nodes.label: Standard report contract
nodes.note: Flat markdown: header table, assessment paragraph, top findings, blockers, findings, clear list, disclaimer. Explicitly no HTML and no colour.

nodes.label: Full-analysis mode contract
nodes.note: Triggered by a keyword. Chapter-by-chapter analysis against the ten-chapter template, per-chapter risk status, score and readiness arithmetic, then a machine-readable payload.

nodes.label: Dashboard payload schema

props.defect: invalid JSON escape sequence in one of the two specifications

nodes.note: document / readiness / riskDistribution / chapters / skills / skillConnections / findings. Specified twice in the source with different escaping: one copy writes ids as doc\_1 and ch\_1. Backslash-underscore is not a valid JSON escape, so a model reproducing that copy literally emits a payload that fails strict parsing.

nodes.label: Full mode: markdown report, then the payload line last

props.quote: Output the STANDARD MODE markdown assessment first (chat display).

nodes.note: Step 4 says output the standard markdown assessment for the chat. Step 5 says the payload line must be the absolute last line of the response.

nodes.label: Full mode: call the action silently and return only its HTML

props.quote: Output nothing else - no markdown, no explanation, no JSON, and no pleasantries. Just the raw HTML.

nodes.note: The same mode is told to construct the payload, call the builder action without showing the JSON, and return nothing but the HTML that comes back.

nodes.label: Business requirements template
nodes.note: The ten-chapter structure every BR is measured against. This is what a BR must contain, not what any one BR says.

nodes.label: Document info
nodes.note: Name, version, requestor, sponsor. Extracted without asking for confirmation.

nodes.label: Stakeholders
nodes.note: Who owns what. Missing names are findings, not blockers.

nodes.label: Fraud and security
nodes.note: Abuse cases and controls.

nodes.label: Business model
nodes.note: Pricing, entitlement and commercial rules. Where contradictions concentrate.

nodes.label: Eligibility
nodes.note: Who may take the product and under what conditions.

nodes.label: Compatibility
nodes.note: What the product may and may not be combined with.

nodes.label: Lifecycle and use cases
nodes.note: The customer journey as ordered use cases. Placeholder use cases are findings.

nodes.label: Migration
nodes.note: Moving an existing base onto the new product.

nodes.label: Reporting
nodes.note: What must be measurable after go-live. Vague metrics are caught here.

nodes.label: Customer documentation
nodes.note: What the customer is told, and where.

nodes.label: detect_contradictions
nodes.note: Two written rules that produce different instructions for the same scenario. Must quote both sides exactly. Runs on every validation before the report is produced.

nodes.label: check_vague_metrics
nodes.note: A target with no number, no unit or no owner. Reporting chapters are the usual source.

nodes.label: check_placeholder_leakage
nodes.note: Template scaffolding left in place and presented as content. Distinguishes an untouched section, which is a scoping decision, from a section that pretends to be filled.

nodes.label: check_completeness
nodes.note: A chapter that is present but says nothing an implementer could act on.

nodes.label: compare_documents
nodes.note: Invoked when two documents are supplied. Looks for conflicting scope, status or rules between them.

nodes.label: write_br
nodes.note: Retrieves the template from the knowledge index and returns it, without asking prerequisite questions.

nodes.label: chapter_deep_dive
nodes.note: Invoked when the requestor asks about one chapter rather than the whole document.

nodes.label: Assistant agent (Copilot Studio)
nodes.note: Holds the system prompt as instructions, the knowledge sources as grounding, and the builder action as a tool. This is the only component that reads the prompt.

nodes.label: Document library
nodes.note: Where the template and the BR documents live. The source of truth a knowledge source points at, not a copy of it.

nodes.label: Knowledge ingestion and indexing

props.note_delay: index refresh lag between editing a document and the agent seeing it

nodes.note: Crawls the library, chunks and indexes the documents, and makes them retrievable by the agent. Re-runs on a schedule, so a template edit is not visible to the agent immediately.

nodes.label: Knowledge index
nodes.note: The retrievable form of the documents. What the agent actually searches; not the documents themselves.

nodes.label: Dashboard builder action
nodes.note: The tool the agent calls with the payload as its single string parameter. The boundary where the payload stops being text and has to be valid JSON.

nodes.label: Dashboard flow
nodes.note: Receives the payload, validates it, and renders the dashboard. Owns the HTML entirely -- which is why the assistant is forbidden from producing any.

nodes.label: Dashboard renderer
nodes.note: Turns the payload into the graph, the dials and the finding list a reviewer reads.

nodes.label: Team chat channel
nodes.note: Where the requestor pastes the document and reads the report.

nodes.label: BR document supplied
nodes.note: A document is pasted or attached. Starts a standard validation with no menu and no confirmation step.

nodes.label: Full-analysis keyword received
nodes.note: The trigger word that switches modes. Anonymised out of this template: the real word is an internal trigger and is not published here.

nodes.label: Idea
nodes.note: A business need is raised, usually by a product or marketing owner. Nothing is committed; it is a candidate.

nodes.label: Pre-analysis
nodes.note: Analysts and platform do a first feasibility pass: is it doable, what does it touch, roughly what is needed.

nodes.label: Portfolio selection
nodes.note: The board reviews candidates and picks which go to delivery: prioritisation, budget, strategic fit.

nodes.label: Kick-off
nodes.note: The approved project starts. Business and legal join the delivery team to align on scope, roles and plan.

nodes.label: Business requirements
nodes.note: The requestor writes the BR: product, use cases, eligibility, channels. This is the stage the assistant validates.

nodes.label: Technical specification
nodes.note: Analysts and platform translate the BR into systems, integrations and data flows.

nodes.label: Build and integrate
nodes.note: Platform and the integration partner implement across the affected systems.

nodes.label: Test
nodes.note: Functional and end-to-end testing, including the pre-production gates.

nodes.label: Go-live
nodes.note: Operations take handover, the product goes live, and the customer journey begins in the channels.

nodes.label: Portfolio selection gate
nodes.note: Decides whether a candidate becomes a project. Budget and strategic fit, not feasibility.

nodes.label: Pre-production test gate
nodes.note: Decides whether a build may go live. The last gate before customers see it.

nodes.label: Business requestor
nodes.note: Raises the idea and writes the BR. Owns the customer proposition.

nodes.label: Business analyst
nodes.note: Bridges business and platform. Owns the technical specification and the human review of a blocked verdict.

nodes.label: Portfolio board
nodes.note: Selects which candidates are funded and delivered.

nodes.label: Legal and compliance
nodes.note: Joins at kick-off and at the BR stage. Owns the legal and data-protection chapters.

nodes.label: Platform team
nodes.note: Builds and integrates. Owns the runtime.

nodes.label: Integration partner
nodes.note: Third party implementing part of the core stack. Outside the operator's change control.

nodes.label: Test team
nodes.note: Runs the gates.

nodes.label: Operations
nodes.note: Takes handover and runs the product in production.

edges.note: Same mode, opposite instruction. One says emit a markdown report and finish with the payload line; the other says emit nothing but the HTML returned by the action, explicitly no markdown and no JSON. An implementer cannot satisfy both and nothing in the document ranks them.

The guardrail forbids producing HTML in any response. The full-analysis rule requires the response to be raw HTML. Reconcilable only by reading 'autonomously' as excluding relayed output -- which is an inference, and the document does not make it.
The topic guardrail fixes one refusal string in a single language. The language rule says the reply mirrors the input. An English off-topic request has two different correct answers.
The payload publishes a 0-100 score as fact. That is the assertion, and it is the one with no evidence behind it.
The template is uploaded to the library, not pasted into the prompt, so it can be revised without touching the assistant.
The prompt is configuration on the agent, not content in the index. Editing it is a change to the agent; editing the template is not.
The template is fetched from the index rather than reproduced from the prompt, which is what keeps one version of it in circulation.
The flow parses the payload. A malformed one fails here, after the analysis has already been done.
The stage where the assistant is used. Every other stage is unaffected by it, which is worth seeing: the tool touches one box in nine.
The technical specification is written from the validated BR plus the report. A blocker reaching this stage means the spec is being written against an undecided rule.
The dashboard is read at selection. This is why the unevidenced score matters: it is presented to the people deciding what gets funded.
The stage cannot complete on a blocked verdict until the review has happened.

logic.goal: Decide whether a business requirement may pass the kick-off gate, and produce the dashboard the selection board reads.

steps.name: Supply the document
steps.intent: A person pastes or attaches the business requirement. There is no menu and no confirmation step -- the arrival of a document is itself the instruction to validate.

steps.name: Extract chapters and rules
steps.intent: Split the document into the ten chapters and pull out every explicit rule and metric, so later steps quote rather than paraphrase.

steps.name: Detect contradictions
steps.intent: Find pairs of written rules that give different instructions for one scenario. Quote both sides exactly.

steps.name: Check vague metrics
steps.intent: Targets with no number, unit or owner.

steps.name: Apply the blocker rule
steps.intent: Sort findings into blockers and findings using the three-case definition. No new judgement; this only applies the rule.

steps.name: Compute score and readiness
steps.intent: Apply the coefficients and the four-dimension mapping to produce the dashboard numbers. Whether those coefficients mean anything is the open claim.

steps.name: Human review of a blocked verdict
steps.intent: A person confirms or overturns before the requestor is told they are blocked. The pipeline stops here.

steps.name: Emit the dashboard payload
steps.intent: Serialise into the schema the builder action accepts. Must be strict JSON.
